subject: AP Environmental Science
source_note: Structured from the AP Environmental Science Course and Exam Description (© 2026). Unit titles follow the CED's framework. Essential questions are written for this app; science-practice descriptions are paraphrased, not quoted.

units.title: Unit 1: The Living World: Ecosystems
essential_questions: Only about ten percent of energy moves up a trophic level. What does that single constraint determine about how ecosystems are shaped?
Is a nutrient cycle better understood as a cycle or as a set of reservoirs with very different residence times?
Two ecosystems have identical primary productivity but different biodiversity. What could explain that?

Read the diagram or model for what it claims, and say where it simplifies
Do the calculation with units on every line, then sanity-check the magnitude
texts: Bring the data set, diagram or article you are working from — paste it and we will read it rather than talk around it

units.title: Unit 2: The Living World: Biodiversity
essential_questions: Ecosystem services are usually argued in dollars. What does that framing win, and what does it concede?
Island biogeography was built from islands. Why does it apply to a national park?
Is a disturbed ecosystem always worse off? Find a case that complicates the answer.

units.title: Unit 3: Populations
essential_questions: Carrying capacity sounds like a fixed number. For humans, is it one?
Two countries with the same total fertility rate can have very different age structures. How?
The demographic transition model was drawn from European history. Where does it fail, and does that make it useless?

units.title: Unit 4: Earth Systems and Resources
essential_questions: Soil takes centuries to form and a season to lose. What does that asymmetry mean for how we should use it?
El Niño is a Pacific phenomenon with global effects. Trace one chain of consequence and say where it weakens.
Watersheds ignore political boundaries. What problems does that create that maps do not show?

units.title: Unit 5: Land and Water Use
essential_questions: The tragedy of the commons assumes people cannot cooperate. Where has that assumption been proved wrong?
Industrial agriculture feeds more people per acre and degrades the acre. How would you decide the trade?
Pick a land use you rely on daily and trace its full environmental cost. What did you not know?

units.title: Unit 6: Energy Resources and Consumption
essential_questions: Every energy source has a hidden cost. Take the one you consider cleanest and argue against it.
Is nuclear power a climate solution or a risk transfer to the future? Defend a position.
Energy conservation is the cheapest source of supply. Why is it the hardest to sell?

units.title: Unit 7: Atmospheric Pollution
essential_questions: Photochemical smog needs sunlight, cars, and geography. Which would you change to fix it fastest?
Indoor air is often worse than outdoor air. Why does regulation focus on the outdoor kind?
Acid rain was substantially solved. What made that possible, and does it transfer to carbon?

units.title: Unit 9: Global Change
essential_questions: The ozone layer is recovering; the climate is not. What is different about the two problems?
Ocean acidification is called the other CO₂ problem. Why does it get less attention, and is that justified?
Invasive species are a global-change symptom that individuals can actually affect. Is that why it is emphasised?
